questions.q: Two linear layers compute $y = W^2(W^1x + b^1) + b^2$. Which single layer gives exactly the same output for every $x$?
options: No single layer can — two layers are strictly more expressive
questions.explain: Distribute $W^2$: $W^2W^1x + W^2b^1 + b^2$. The order matters ($W^2W^1$, not $W^1W^2$) and the first bias is also multiplied by $W^2$.

questions.q: In Lab 1 you stack 8 linear layers whose hidden width is 1 (2 → 1 → … → 1 → 2), with no activation. What does the output grid look like?
options: A rotated and stretched but still 2-D grid
All points lie on a single line, because $\operatorname{rank}(W_\text{eff}) \le 1$
It depends on how many layers there are
questions.explain: The rank of a product is at most the smallest rank of its factors. A width-1 layer has rank ≤ 1, so the collapsed 2×2 map has rank ≤ 1 and squeezes the plane onto a line — no amount of depth can undo it.

questions.q: Why can a 10-layer network with **no** activation functions not solve XOR?
options: It collapses to $W_\text{eff}x + b_\text{eff}$, whose decision boundary is a single straight line
Gradient descent cannot train networks deeper than 2 layers
XOR needs a sigmoid output; linear nets have none
questions.explain: However many parameters the stack has, the function equals one linear layer, and no straight line separates the XOR corners. One hidden ReLU layer can carve out the needed band.

questions.q: LoRA fine-tunes a frozen weight $W$ with a low-rank update $BA$ ($B$: $d\times r$, $A$: $r\times d$). Why is there no extra inference cost after training?
options: $B(Ax)$ is a stack of linear maps with no activation, so it merges into one matrix $W' = W + BA$
LoRA adds a ReLU that is cheap to compute
questions.explain: This is the collapse used on purpose: $Wx + B(Ax) = (W + BA)x$. The adapter is a deliberately low-rank linear factorization that can be folded back into $W$.
